summary: General European conventions for cross-border applications. Where a specific country is known, its own profile should be used instead — this profile is the sane default for applications that cross borders, such as EU institutions, Erasmus programmes and pan-European employers.

photo.note: Photo expectations differ sharply inside Europe: common in German-speaking countries and some southern states, unusual in the UK, Ireland and the Nordics. When in doubt, leave it out — an application without a photo is never penalised for that reason alone.

personalInfo.note: Nationality is sometimes relevant for work-permit purposes within the EU; date of birth and marital status generally are not. GDPR gives you the right to withhold personal data that is not necessary for the application.

page.note: Two pages for most roles; the Europass-style format often runs longer because language and digital-skill grids take space.

notes: A single-column, photo-free version is the safest choice for large employers and for any application that crosses a border.
The Europass format is one widely used European structure, not a legal requirement — no European country mandates a specific CV format.
State language proficiency explicitly, ideally with a CEFR level (A1–C2) — European recruiters read these directly.
An English CV is accepted by most pan-European employers, but a CV in the employer's language is a meaningful advantage.

advisories.text: European recruiters are usually familiar with CEFR levels, so listing them next to each language often makes an application easier to compare across borders.
Europass is a widely recognised European format, not the only correct one. A well-structured two-page CV is equally acceptable to most employers.
Under the GDPR you may withhold data that is not necessary for the application; recruiters may not require a photo or date of birth.
If you need a work permit, a one-line statement of your current status prevents early screening questions.
